title: Russian placement diagnostic (Мир, custom track), stage 1
notes: Item bank for docs/russian-mir-custom-design.md §6.1, in the format of content/grc/diagnostic/FORMAT.md with the Russian deltas listed in content/ru-mirc/diagnostic/authoring-notes.md (sources, word counts, tag list, sampling, answer checks, doubts). No stress marks anywhere; ё printed where standard.

sections.title: About you
sections.intro_en: This short test helps choose where the course's reading starts and shows where Russian reading gets hard. The core is three passages with five questions each (about 15 minutes), then a page where you mark the places that stopped you. An optional 8-minute section on words and forms follows. Nothing here is timed, and you can stop at any section break and come back. First, one untimed practice round. Typing needs a Russian keyboard layout; stress marks are never needed, and е for ё is fine.

sections.title: Reading
sections.intro_en: Three passages, each a little harder than the one before: a story written for this test, a shortened story by Tolstoy, and a short piece by Turgenev exactly as he wrote it. Read at your own pace; the text stays on screen while you answer, and rereading is expected. A few rarer words are glossed under each passage. If a question can't be answered, leave it rather than guess.

sections.title: Where did you get stuck?
sections.intro_en: Mark up to five places where your reading stopped, and say what you think they mean, even if that is 'no idea'. Help then arrives in steps: a few word meanings, then the shape of the sentence, then a translation.

sections.title: Optional: words and forms
sections.intro_en: About 8 minutes. Words in short Russian sentences (pick the meaning and say how sure you are; 'unknown' is a perfectly good answer), mixed with gaps where you type a form of the word given in brackets. The section ends by itself after three blanks or 'unknown's in a row; that is expected, not a failure.

practice.label: Practice
practice.context_en: A warm-up: two sentences about a boy and his dog.

sentences.translation_en: Sharik runs to the river.
The boy walks after him and laughs.

options: The boy is following Sharik.
Sharik is following the boy.
The boy and Sharik are walking side by side.
The boy is following his father.
why: Right: мальчик идёт за ним, 'the boy goes after him', and ним is Шарик.
Шарик runs ahead to the river; за ним puts the boy behind.
за ним is 'after him', not 'with him'.
There is no father here; ним refers back to Шарик.

options: found
lost
buried
chewed

practice.ablation: n/a (lexical item; the sentence is built so that all four options fit it)

p1.label: Нина едет к бабушке (written for this test)
p1.source: new narrative written for this diagnostic at the level of the later LingQ Mini Stories (past-tense retelling, everyday vocabulary)
p1.context_en: A young woman who has moved to Moscow hears from her grandmother in the village.

sentences.translation_en: Last autumn Nina moved to Moscow.
She found a job in a big shop and rented a small flat not far from the centre.
The work was hard, and in the evenings Nina got very tired.
One Saturday she received a letter from her grandmother.
Grandmother lived in a village and didn't like the telephone, so she always wrote letters.
Nina began reading the letter on the bus but didn't finish it: she had to get off.

clauses.label: explanation: she had to get off

sentences.translation_en: At home she read it to the end.
Grandmother wrote that her cat had had kittens and that she had already given two kittens to children from the school.
She also wrote that she missed her and was really looking forward to Nina's visit.
Nina thought: "I haven't been to Grandmother's for a whole year!"
On Monday she asked her boss for three days off.
At first the boss didn't want to let her go, but then he agreed.
On Friday Nina bought presents: a warm shawl for Grandmother and sweets for the neighbours' children.
In the morning she got on the train, and from the station to the village she walked.
She crossed the river by the old bridge, went round a big field and entered the village.
Grandmother was standing by the house, talking with some neighbours.
When she saw Nina, at first she didn't believe her eyes, and then she burst into tears of joy.

p1-q1.prompt_en: What happens in this passage, in brief?
options: Nina, who now lives in Moscow, gets a letter from her grandmother, takes a few days off and goes to the village to see her.
Nina's grandmother moves to Moscow to be near her, and Nina meets her at the station with presents for her and the neighbours.
Nina writes to her grandmother every week, and one Friday her grandmother comes to Moscow by train to stay for three days.
Nina loses her job at the shop in Moscow and goes back by train to live with her grandmother in the village.
why: Right: письмо от бабушки, три выходных дня, поезд, деревня.
Nina moved to Moscow (переехала); her grandmother lives in the village and stays there.
It is the grandmother who writes (всегда писала письма), and Nina goes to her.
Nina keeps her job: the boss lets her go for three days (согласился).
p1-q1.ablation: The gist depends on following the chain of main verbs and their subjects (переехала, получила, попросила, села, вошла); a reader who loses who moved, who wrote and who travelled picks B–D.

p1-q2.prompt_en: Where did Nina finish reading the letter?
options: At home
On the bus
At work
She never finished it
why: Right: on the bus она начала читать … но не дочитала; at home она прочитала его до конца.
не дочитала: she did not get to the end on the bus; that is where she only began (начала читать).
Work is not where she read it; the letter came on a Saturday and she read it on the bus and at home.
The bus reading was cut short, but дома она прочитала его до конца.
p1-q2.ablation: The answer rests on telling начала читать / не дочитала (began, did not complete) from прочитала до конца (completed); if all three are just 'read', B and C stay open.

p1-q3.prompt_en: What did Grandmother's letter say about the kittens?
options: Her cat had had kittens, and she had already given two of them to some children from the school.
Some children from the school had given her two kittens for her cat to look after.
Her cat had had kittens, but she had not given any away yet.
She had taken two of the kittens to the school to show the children.
why: Right: она уже отдала двух котят детям из школы — детям is 'to (the) children'.
The subject of отдала is она (Grandmother); детям is dative plural, the people who receive.
уже отдала: she had already given two away.
из школы says which children, not where she took the kittens; отдала means 'gave (away)'.
p1-q3.ablation: Only the dative plural ending of детям marks the children as the receivers rather than the givers (B); the aspect and adverb of уже отдала exclude C.

p1-q4.prompt_en: How did Nina get from the station into the village?
options: On foot: she crossed the river by the old bridge, went round a big field and walked into the village.
On foot: she walked along the river as far as the old bridge, went straight across a big field and came into the village.
On foot: she crossed the river by the old bridge, went straight across a big field and walked on past the village.
By bus: it crossed the river by the old bridge and drove round a big field into the village.
why: Right: перешла через реку (across), обошла поле (round), вошла в деревню (in).
пере- with через реку is 'across' the river, and об- in обошла is 'round' the field, not across it.
об- is 'round' the field, and в- in вошла в деревню is 'into', not past.
от станции до деревни шла пешком: she walked.
p1-q4.ablation: B and C differ from A only in what the prefixes пере- (across), об- (round) and в- (into) say about the route; пешком rules out D.

p1-q5.prompt_en: What was Grandmother doing when Nina arrived, and how did she react?
options: She was standing by the house talking with some neighbours; at first she couldn't believe her eyes, then she burst into tears of joy.
She was standing by the house talking with some neighbours; she did not recognise Nina, so she carried on talking.
When she saw Nina she went to stand by the house and talk with the neighbours; only later did she cry with joy.
She was talking with the neighbours and had been crying with joy all along, even before Nina came.
why: Right: стояла … разговаривала (ongoing when Nina came); не поверила своим глазам, then заплакала (began to cry).
не поверила своим глазам: she could not believe her eyes, not that she failed to recognise her.
стояла and разговаривала are imperfective: what she was already doing at that moment, not new steps after seeing Nina.
заплакала is perfective with за-: she began to cry at that point, after first not believing it.
p1-q5.ablation: C and D are what a reader gets by treating the imperfectives стояла/разговаривала as new events in sequence, or the perfective заплакала (began to cry) as a state that was already going on.

p2.label: По Л. Н. Толстому, «Прыжок» (shortened)
p2.source: L. N. Tolstoy, «Прыжок», a story for children (dated 1880 on Wikisource). Text: Собрание сочинений в 22 т., т. 10, М.: Художественная литература, 1982, via ru.wikisource.org/wiki/Прыжок_(Толстой). Public domain. Shortened from about 530 to about 240 words; see authoring-notes.md for every change.
p2.context_en: A story by Tolstoy for children, shortened. A sailing ship is on its way home, and the whole crew is on deck.

sentences.translation_en: A ship had sailed round the world and was returning home.
All the people were on deck.
In the middle of the crowd a big monkey was spinning about and amusing everyone.
It jumped up to a twelve-year-old boy, the captain's son, tore the hat off his head and nimbly climbed up the mast.
Everyone burst out laughing, and the boy went red, threw off his jacket and rushed up the mast after the monkey.
In one minute the monkey and the boy got right to the top.
There the monkey hung the hat on the end of the crossbar, while it climbed onto the very tip of the mast and bared its teeth from there.
There was no way to reach the hat except by letting go of the rope and the mast.
But the boy let go of the mast and stepped onto the crossbar.
On deck everyone was watching and laughing; but when they saw him walking along the crossbar, balancing with his arms, they all froze with fear.
He had only to miss his footing, and he would have been smashed to pieces against the deck.
At that moment the captain, the boy's father, came out of the cabin.
He was carrying a gun to shoot gulls.
He saw his son on the mast, at once took aim at him and shouted: "Into the water! Jump into the water! I'll shoot!"
The boy was swaying, but did not understand.
"Jump or I'll shoot! One, two…" — and as soon as his father shouted "three", the boy jumped head first.
The waves had not yet closed over him when twenty sailors had already jumped from the ship into the sea.
About forty seconds later (they seemed long to everyone) the boy's body came up to the surface.
They pulled him out onto the ship, and a few minutes later he began to breathe.
When the captain saw this, he suddenly cried out as if something were choking him, and ran off to his cabin so that no one would see him crying.

p2-q1.prompt_en: What happens in this passage, in brief?
options: A monkey snatches the captain's son's hat; chasing it, the boy ends up on a high crossbar, and his father makes him jump into the sea at gunpoint, where sailors rescue him.
A monkey steals the captain's hat and climbs the mast; the captain comes out with a gun and shoots at the monkey, and his son, who has climbed after it, falls into the sea.
The captain's son climbs the mast for a bet with the sailors; he slips on the crossbar and falls onto the deck, and the sailors carry him to his father's cabin.
A monkey falls from the top of the mast into the sea, and the captain's son jumps in to save it while the sailors laugh; the captain then fishes them both out.
why: Right: сорвала … шляпу, бросился за обезьяной, прицелился в него, прыгнул, вытащили на корабль.
The hat is the boy's (с его головы, his = the boy's), and the father aims at his son, not the monkey.
There is no bet, and he does not fall: the danger is what would happen if he did (он бы разбился); he jumps into the sea.
The monkey stays on top of the mast; it is the boy who goes into the sea.
p2-q1.ablation: The gist depends on following who does what in the chain of main clauses (сорвала, бросился, ступил, прицелился, прыгнул, спрыгнули, вытащили); a reader who takes the unreal разбился as fact or loses the subjects picks B–D.

p2-q2.prompt_en: What does «Стоило ему только оступиться — и он бы вдребезги разбился о палубу» tell us?
options: One false step, and he would have been smashed to pieces on the deck.
He missed his footing and was smashed to pieces on the deck.
He only had to step down onto the deck, and he would be safe.
Missing his footing cost him dearly: he was badly hurt on the deck.
why: Right: стоило … только + infinitive, 'it would only have taken …', and бы makes разбился an outcome that did not happen.
бы makes разбился unreal: what would have happened. He is still on the crossbar in the next sentences.
оступиться is to miss one's footing, not to step down; the deck is where he would have landed.
стоило here is not 'cost'; and бы means the fall did not happen.
p2-q2.ablation: Without бы, разбился reads as a real event (B, D); only the particle (with стоило … только) marks the fall as unreal. оступиться and вдребезги are glossed under the passage so the item turns on the construction.

p2-q3.prompt_en: What did the sailors do, and when?
options: Before the waves had even closed over the boy, twenty sailors had already jumped from the ship into the sea.
They waited until the waves had closed over the boy, and then twenty of them jumped into the sea.
Twenty sailors climbed down the mast after the boy before he hit the water.
The waves were too high for them, so twenty sailors stayed on the ship and threw down ropes.
why: Right: Не успели волны закрыть его, как уже … спрыгнули: the sailors were in before the waves closed.
Не успели …, как уже puts the jump before the waves had time to close, not after.
спрыгнули с корабля в море: they jumped off the ship into the sea; the boy was already in the water.
It is the waves that 'did not have time' (не успели волны), not the sailors who failed.
p2-q3.ablation: Не успели X, как уже Y places Y before X is complete; read as two plain past statements it gives B or D, and the direction с корабля в море excludes C.

p2-q4.prompt_en: What happened after about forty seconds?
options: The boy's body came up to the surface.
The boy's body sank out of sight.
The sailors dived down after the boy's body.
The boy swam back to the ship by himself.
why: Right: вы- 'out' + нырнуть 'dive': the body came up out of the water.
вы- means out: the body came out of the water, not down into it.
тело мальчика is the subject of вынырнуло (subject after the verb); the sailors are not in this sentence.
He is pulled out (вытащили), and only then starts to breathe.
p2-q4.ablation: With нырять 'to dive' glossed under the passage, only the prefix вы- ('out') separates surfacing (A) from diving down (B, C).

p2-q5.prompt_en: Why did the captain run off to his cabin?
options: So that no one would see him crying.
To put the gun away before anyone saw it.
Because he could not bear to watch the sailors trying to bring his son round.
Because nobody had noticed that he was crying.
why: Right: чтобы никто не видел, как он плачет: purpose.
The gun is not mentioned again; the purpose clause is about his crying.
His son was already breathing (он стал дышать) when he ran off.
чтобы gives a purpose, 'so that'; it is not что, 'that'.
p2-q5.ablation: чтобы никто не видел states a purpose; read as что ('that') it turns into the statement in D, and the reason for running off is lost.

p3.label: И. С. Тургенев, «Воробей» (1878)
p3.source: I. S. Turgenev, «Воробей», from Стихотворения в прозе (Senilia), dated April 1878, first published in Вестник Европы, 1882. Text: Полное собрание сочинений и писем в 30 т., Сочинения т. 10, via ru.wikisource.org/wiki/Воробей_(Тургенев). Public domain. Complete and unchanged except that ё is printed where standard.
p3.context_en: A complete prose poem by Turgenev, as he wrote it. The narrator is walking home through a garden with his hunting dog.

sentences.translation_en: I was coming back from hunting and walking along an avenue of the garden.
My dog was running ahead of me.
Suddenly he slowed his pace and began to creep, as if he had scented game in front of him.
I glanced along the avenue and saw a young sparrow with yellow round its beak and down on its head.
It had fallen out of the nest (the wind was shaking the birches of the avenue hard) and was sitting motionless, helplessly spreading its barely sprouting little wings.

My dog was slowly approaching it when suddenly, breaking away from a nearby tree, an old black-breasted sparrow dropped like a stone right in front of his muzzle — and, all ruffled, distorted, with a desperate and pitiful squeak, it hopped twice or so towards the toothy open jaws.
It rushed to save, it shielded its offspring with itself… but its whole little body was trembling with horror, its little voice had gone wild and hoarse, it was faint, it was sacrificing itself!
What a huge monster the dog must have seemed to it!
And yet it could not stay sitting on its high, safe branch…
A force stronger than its will threw it down from there.
My Trezor stopped and backed away… Evidently he too acknowledged this force.
I hurried to call off the abashed dog — and walked away, full of reverence.
Yes; don't laugh.
I felt reverence before that small heroic bird, before its loving impulse.
Love, I thought, is stronger than death and the fear of death.
Only by it, only by love does life hold together and move.

p3-q1.prompt_en: What happens in this passage, in brief?
options: A young sparrow has fallen from its nest; as the narrator's dog creeps up to it, an old sparrow throws itself down in front of the dog to protect it, the dog backs away, and the narrator, moved, calls the dog off.
The narrator's dog catches a young sparrow that has fallen from its nest, although an old sparrow flies down and tries to drive the dog away, and the narrator, upset, leaves the garden.
An old sparrow pushes a young one out of the nest to teach it to fly; the narrator's dog creeps up, but the young bird flies off, and the narrator laughs at the dog.
The narrator finds a young sparrow that has fallen from its nest, chases off his dog when it creeps up, and puts the bird back in the nest, moved by its courage.
why: Right: упал из гнезда; старый воробей камнем упал перед … мордой; Трезор … попятился; я поспешил отозвать … пса.
The dog does not catch anything: it stops and backs away (остановился, попятился).
The wind shook the birches and the young bird fell (упал); it was not pushed, and it cannot fly (сидел неподвижно).
It is the old sparrow that faces the dog down; the narrator only calls his dog off and leaves, and nobody touches the young bird.
p3-q1.ablation: The gist depends on keeping the two sparrows apart and following the main verbs through the participle and verbal-adverb phrases (упал, приближалась, упал, прыгнул, заслонил, остановился, попятился, отозвать).

p3-q2.prompt_en: What were the young sparrow's wings like?
options: They had barely begun to grow.
They had been broken in the fall.
They were fully grown, and it was beating them to fly back up.
They had been torn by the wind.
why: Right: едва прораставшие крылышки, 'little wings that were barely sprouting'.
Nothing is broken: it sat still, wings spread (растопырив).
It sat without moving (сидел неподвижно); its wings were only just growing.
The wind shook the birches (качал берёзы); it did not damage the wings.
p3-q2.ablation: The only description of the wings is the participle прораставшие ('that were sprouting', with едва 'barely'); прорастать is glossed, so the item turns on reading the participle as an adjective on крылышки.

p3-q3.prompt_en: Who came down from the nearby tree, and how?
options: The old sparrow: it dropped like a stone right in front of the dog's muzzle.
The young sparrow: it fell like a stone straight into the dog's open jaws.
A stone, knocked off the tree by the old sparrow, which fell in front of the dog's muzzle.
The old sparrow: it flew down slowly and landed on the dog's head.
why: Right: сорвавшись с близкого дерева shares its subject with упал: старый черногрудый воробей. камнем is 'like a stone'.
The young bird was already on the ground (упал из гнезда, сидел неподвижно); сорвавшись goes with the old sparrow.
камнем is instrumental of manner, 'like a stone': no stone falls.
камнем упал: it dropped, not flew slowly; перед самой её мордой is 'right in front of her muzzle'.
p3-q3.ablation: сорвавшись has no subject of its own; it takes the subject of the main verb упал (старый воробей). Attaching it to the young sparrow gives B, and reading камнем as a noun subject gives C.

p3-q4.prompt_en: In «Каким громадным чудовищем должна была ему казаться собака!», who seemed what to whom?
options: The dog must have seemed a huge monster to the old sparrow.
The old sparrow, in its fury, must have seemed a huge monster to the dog.
The narrator must have seemed a huge monster to the old sparrow.
The dog must have seemed a huge monster to the young sparrow.
why: Right: собака (nominative) is what seemed; ему (dative) is the one it seemed to, the old sparrow the paragraph is about; чудовищем (instrumental) is what it seemed.
This swaps the roles: собака is nominative, the one that seems; ему, 'to him', is the sparrow.
The narrator is not in this sentence; собака is its subject.
ему continues the old sparrow of the sentences before (он ринулся … он жертвовал собою); the young one is not mentioned here.
p3-q4.ablation: The cases decide between A, B and C: собака nominative (who seems), ему dative (to whom), чудовищем instrumental (seems what); swapping them gives B, missing the subject gives C. D tests whether ему is tracked back to the old sparrow.

options: The dog stops and backs away; the narrator hurries to call the abashed dog off and walks away, full of reverence.
The dog stops and backs away; the narrator calls the dog over to him and then goes up to the birds, feeling embarrassed.
The dog stops and backs away; the narrator hurries to pick up the young sparrow and carries it off reverently.
The dog keeps creeping forward; the narrator urges it on, then turns away in embarrassment.
why: Right: остановился, попятился (backed away); отозвать (call off); смущённого пса (the abashed dog); удалился (went away), благоговея.
от- in отозвать is 'away, off', and у- in удалился is 'away': he leaves the birds. It is the dog that is abashed (смущённого пса).
He touches nothing: he calls the dog away (отозвать) and leaves (удалился).
по-пятиться is to back away; and смущённого describes the dog (пса), not the narrator.
p3-q5.ablation: The ending is carried by prefixed verbs (попятиться 'back away', отозвать 'call off', удалиться 'move away') and the participle смущённого (agreeing with пса). Read as their roots ('heel', 'call', 'far') and with the participle on the wrong noun, B–D are as good as A.
